newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori insists crisis a isolated event.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori insists crisis a isolated event.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori insisted on Thursday that Peru's hostage crisis was an isolated event and condemned the Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence.
The 16-day-old siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence was "an isolated event that is not going to upset the Peruvian economy," Fujimori said in his second public speech since the crisis began.
In an energetic 15-minute message clearly intended to restore confidence in the country's battered reputation, Fujimori gave no clues about his next steps in the crisis.
He attacked the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) premise that it was fighting for Peru's impoverished masses.

"It is an error to think that the violence that arises from discontent can end poverty," Fujimori said. "Twelve years of violence from Sendero Luminoso (guerrillas) and the MRTA -- feverish, destructive violence -- has, on the contrary, made us poorer."
The guerrillas "cannot say that by destroying factories, bridges and by chasing away investors and tourists, poverty is going to be reduced," he said.

Fujimori, whose popularity ratings were tumbling before the crisis as Peru suffered increasing economic difficulties and a series of disasters, including two massive air crashes and an earthquake, qualified 1996 as "a very difficult year."
He said the government would spend 1997 working for "peace and employment."
The crisis moved into a more precarious phase on Thursday after a trickle of hostage releases left the defiant MRTA guerrillas holding 74 hostages who they viewed as their most valuable.
The rebels have vowed to use them as bargaining chips for their principal demand -- the release of all their roughly 400 comrades in Peruvian jails.
"We'll hold them there as long as it takes," Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) international spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters in an interview from Germany.

"The guerrillas can stand it -- they've been trained in the jungle. But can the hostages? If they suffer, the Peruvian government must accept all responsibility for not facilitating a solution to this situation."
Fujimori has flatly rejected the rebels' demands, although he has said "several options" were being looked at to try to end the crisis.
While Wednesday's release of seven hostages, including four Japanese businessmen, was widely welcomed, it was also interpreted as leaving the rebels in a more sharply defined and dangerous position.
More than 500 people were initially taken hostage at the compound. All females and elderly men caught in the siege were released within a short time and many others were let go over the next 16 days.
"The situation is becoming more tense as the number of hostages nears a level the guerrillas can control," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo.

The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, two foreign ambassadors, a host of high-ranking government officials and security force top brass, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Continuing their slick media blitz, the rebels called on world opinion on Thursday to press for a bloodless end to the standoff, which began on December 17, and challenged Fujimori to make a move.

"We ask the progressive men and women of the world to continue demanding of the Peruvian government a political solution which will bring the freedom of (rebel) political prisoners and the prisoners of war taken by our commando unit," the MRTA said in a communique sent to Reuters from "somewhere in the central jungle" of Peru before Fujimori's speech.
"It is the Peruvian government's turn to speak," it added.

Fujimori, angered by an impromptu news conference given by the rebels inside the compound on New Year's Eve, had not spoken publicly since a December 21 speech and has kept his negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, out of the building since Saturday's first meeting with the rebels.
Using sharply different methods, both sides have waged a fierce propaganda battle throughout the crisis.

The government has cut off the residence's communication links and mostly kept journalists two blocks away from the compound, while the MRTA has used methods from cardboard placards to the Internet to get their demands across.

Fujimori was furious at the rebels' propaganda coup on Tuesday -- inviting a group of photographers and cameramen into the residence -- and spent New Year's Day cloistered at Government Palace with security advisers.
